bugs: The mention regex `(?<![\w@])@(\w+)` stops at '.' or '-', so if a username like 'john.doe' ever existed, '@john.doe' would notify user 'john' instead. Nothing validates usernames, but this implementation's own factory (`regexify('[a-z][a-z0-9_]{7,11}')`) only produces \w usernames, so the factory and the parser agree. This is a latent problem, not one the app can hit today.
antipatterns: app/Mail/MentionedInReply.php:21-22 builds the HTML body by string-concatenating `e()` calls into `Content(htmlString:)` instead of using a Blade or markdown view.

database/migrations/2026_11_07_205204_add_username_to_users_table.php:12 makes `username` nullable even though the task asks for a unique username on every user (acceptable for existing rows, but nothing enforces it).

app/Actions/CreateReply.php:27-30 sends mail synchronously in a loop after commit. One SMTP failure gives a 500 for a reply that was already saved and skips the remaining recipients. The other two implementations behave the same way.
strengths: A thin invokable controller delegates to a single-purpose `CreateReply` action. Mail and notifications go out only after `DB::transaction` commits, and `reply_count` is incremented inside the same transaction.
`thread->replies()->make()` plus `user()->associate()` keeps `user_id` and `thread_id` out of `$fillable`, which is a tight mass-assignment surface.
`Reply::mentionedUsers()` uses `collect()->map->unique` and `whereKeyNot` to drop the author. It lowercases usernames to match the lowercasing `Attribute` mutator on User.
The factory's username pattern matches the mention parser.

These are the strongest tests: guest JSON and plain requests both get 401; validation messages are asserted; the reply count is checked after two posts; each recipient gets exactly one mail with exactly one `to`; the failure path asserts no mail, no notification and a rolled-back counter; email addresses are not treated as mentions; the mailable's subject and escaped HTML are rendered and checked.

bugs: The UserFactory uses `fake()->unique()->userName()`, which in a probe produced dotted usernames (for example 'jovani.ortiz') for 113 of 200 users. The mention regex `@(\w+)` in app/Models/Reply.php:34 cannot match those names. In the probe, '@john.doe' never notified user 'john.doe' and instead emailed and notified user 'john'. Most factory-made users therefore cannot be mentioned, and the wrong user can be notified.
antipatterns: app/Models/Reply.php:34 and database/factories/UserFactory.php define the username format differently (`\w+` versus faker usernames that contain dots), and nothing validates the username format.
app/Actions/PostReply.php:27-30 sends mail synchronously in a loop. A transport failure leaves the reply saved but returns a 500 and skips the remaining recipients.
strengths: The structure is clean: a resource-style `ThreadReplyController@store` and a `PostReply` action. The transaction wraps the reply insert and the counter increment, and notifications are sent after commit.
Relationship-based creation with `associate()` keeps foreign keys out of `$fillable`.
The mailable uses a plain-text Blade view rather than inline HTML.

The tests are thorough. They assert exact validation messages, check that each mail has exactly one `to` and empty cc and bcc, cover self-mentions, unknown names and email addresses, and check that a failed write leaves the counter and notifications untouched. They never use the factory's own usernames in a mention, so they miss the dotted-username mismatch.

antipatterns: app/Http/Controllers/ReplyController.php:19-44 puts the transaction, mention lookup and mail/notification fan-out directly in the controller instead of an action or the model.

app/Models/Reply.php:34 uses `array_values(array_unique(array_map('strtolower', …)))` where a collection pipeline would be clearer. User.php also uses `strtolower` instead of `Str::lower` or `mb_strtolower`.
app/Models/Reply.php:11 and app/Models/Thread.php:12 make `user_id`, `thread_id` and `reply_count` mass-assignable. `reply_count` should never be fillable.
app/Models/Thread.php:18 sets `$attributes` to `reply_count => 0`, which duplicates the column's database default.
app/Mail/MentionedInReply.php:14 and app/Notifications/MentionedInReply.php:11 include `Queueable` and `SerializesModels` boilerplate, but neither class implements `ShouldQueue`.
app/Http/Controllers/ReplyController.php:33 adds an `if ($usernames !== [])` guard that does little except save one query.
strengths: The mention regex `@([A-Za-z0-9_.-]*[A-Za-z0-9_])` handles dotted and hyphenated usernames, which faker's `userName()` produces, and ignores trailing punctuation. In the probe, '@john.doe' correctly notified john.doe and not john.
Notifications go out only after `DB::transaction` commits, the counter is incremented inside the transaction, and the author is excluded with `whereKeyNot`.
The mailable uses a markdown view with `x-mail::message`.
The migration's down() drops the unique index before dropping the column.

The tests cover the unique and lowercase username constraint (a duplicate with different case throws `UniqueConstraintViolationException`), the failure path with both fakes, a one-recipient check with no cc or bcc, and a reply with no mentions. The validation assertions are weaker: they check only the status code, not the messages.

v.rationale:
All three suites pass (12 tests each). All three create the reply and increment `reply_count` inside `DB::transaction`, then send mail and notifications after commit. Each mentioned user gets one email addressed only to them and one database notification. In every implementation a failing `Reply::creating` sent nothing, which my probes confirmed. Punctuation and mixed-case mentions such as '(@alice), @BOB.' worked in all three, as did real (unfaked) mail delivery to a single recipient.

The difference came from the dotted-username probe. impl-2's UserFactory uses faker `userName()`, which produced dotted names for 113 of 200 users, but its parser only matches `\w+`. So '@john.doe' notified user 'john' and never 'john.doe'. That is an internal inconsistency and a real bug that sends a notification to the wrong person. impl-1 has the same parser, but its factory only generates `[a-z0-9_]` usernames, so the two agree and the problem is only latent. impl-3's parser handles dots and hyphens correctly, so it is the most correct, but its code is less idiomatic: the logic sits in the controller, the arrays are handled with `array_*` functions, `reply_count` and the foreign keys are fillable, `$attributes` repeats the database default, and the mailable and notification carry unused `Queueable`/`SerializesModels` traits.

impl-1 ranks first. It has a clean action-based design, a tight mass-assignment surface, a factory that matches its parser, and the most complete tests, including a render test for the mailable. impl-3 is second because it is the most correct but carries more ceremony and weaker idioms. impl-2 is third: its design is nearly identical to impl-1's, but the mismatch between its factory and its parser is a real bug.
